ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS  
Setting up leather Parks  
* 181. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPRAft 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGROD1A: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is considering setting up Leather Parks in the country; 
(b) if so, the details of the scheme and what fiscal and financial incentives shall be given 
to these Parks; 
(c) whether locations of such Parks have been identified; 
(d) if so, who identifies the location, and what is the size of such Parks; 
(e) who will be responsible for developing the infrastructure in such Parks; and 
(f) what will be the role and obligations of the respective State Governments? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY   (SHRI KAMAL  NATH): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
(e) Special Purpose Vehicle would be responsible for developing the infrastructure in the 
parks/complexes. 
(f) The State Governments or its agencies may participate in the project by providing 
necessary assistance for infrastructure, power, water and other utilities.

SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: The Minister has said in t he answer that the State 
Government and its agencies may participate in the project by providing necessary assistance 
for infrastructure, power, water and other utilities. Sir, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether adequate steps have been ensured by way of providing power and water in 
order to keep the public, in the vicinity of the leather parks, free of pollution. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, concerns relating to envir onment are paramount and 
foremost in the Government's policies and the way w e implement them. There can be no 
doubt that while we have to assure water, power and other facilities to the leather sector, we 
also have to be mindful of the concerns of the residents relating to pollution and environment. 
I would like to assure the hon. Member that in impl ementing our policies, these concerns 
will be the foremost. 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister, apart 
from the Special Purpose Vehicle responsible for developing the infrastructure, would there 
be any machinery involved in keeping proper vigil o n the safe functioning of the leather 
parks and proper health care of the workers working therein. I also would like to know how 
many State Governments and their agencies have participated in this project so far. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, the position as regards th e participation of the State 
Governments have been given in the statement annexed to my answer with respect to the 
Tenth Plan. With respect to the Eleventh Plan, we t hink that this is going to be extended 
much further because the Plan allocation has been raised from Rs. 400 Crores to Rs. 1,300 
Crores; that is what is under consideration of the Expenditure finance Committee. As far as 
the concerns of the health workers is concerned, qu ite clearly, this is again a foremost 
consideration and the appropriate agencies do take care to ensure that the minimal standards 
of health care are observed. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, the hon. Minister has not yet replied on who identified 
the locations, because he has given only three locations. I would like to know if they have 
any plan for many more locations because three locations are not enough. Also, Sir, in the 
Tenth Plan, what kind of finance was allocated in the Budget? I understand that nothing has 
been utilised. For the Eleventh Plan also it has been trebled. But, will it, at all, be utilised? 
What is the plan of the Government so that these funds do not go unutilised and what kind of 
subsidy is being given? who is getting the subsidy? What is the procedure for subsidy? 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, in the Tenth Plan, the methodology adopted, and which 
is going to be continued in the Eleventh Plan as well as the Special Purpose Vehicle which

could be either by a public sector corporation or by public-private partnership, or it could be 
by the private sector. As I have indicated in my statement, for example, we have got three 
parks, one in Kolkata and two in Chennai. The Special purpose Vehicles have been identified. 
In one place, it is a consortium of private entrepreneurs, and in another case it is the State 
Government agency, and that would be what would be carried forward in the Eleventh Plan. 
Sir, it is true that as far as the allocation of th e funds earmarked in the Tenth Plan is 
concerned, there was some under-utilisation and the reason was that the scheme was notified 
only in November. So, we lost 7-8 months. Therefore, there was a small under-utilisation of 
the amount it is equally true. Sir that for the Ele venth Five Year Plan, we have raised the 
limit as I said, from Rs. 400 crores to Rs. 1,300 c rores. That is the estimated perspective 
Plan which we hope will be finalised. As far as the  site selections, is concerned, that is a 
function of the Special Purpose Vehicle because, as the hon. Chairman knows, this activity 
is concentrated in certain States and the most suit able site available is identified by the 
company, which is the Special Purpose Vehicle, which takes all factors into consideration. 
SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like the hon. Minister 
to give me information about the other States which have applied for permission for setting 
up of leather parks and whether the Government of Maharasthra has requested for permission 
for establishment of such a park. If so, when was it submitted and what is its present status? 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, as we are now in the beginning of the Eleventh Plan, the 
schemes for the Eleventh Plan are yet to be receive d and as and when all the States have 
applied, different States have applied. I will submit the information as far as Eleventh Plan 
is concerned. With regard to Tenth pl an..(interruptions)...  
SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, my question was different. My question was, how many 
applications have come from different States so far. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, in the Eleventh Plan we have not received any application 
because the Plan itself has not been finalised. 
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Sir, through you, what I would 
like to know from the hon. Minister is this. There is one Goods Export Leather Park in 
Kolkata as has been mentioned in the answer and the assistance from the Central Government 
is Rs. 5 crores. According to the information, the Special Purpose Vehicle with West Bengal 
will perform. My speitic question is: (a) What is the present states of the Goods Export Park; 
and, (b) is there any time frame when a will start and when it will be completed? 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, the Leather Park in Kolkata is at its final stages. It is 
expected to be completed by the end of 2007-08. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. It has been conceded by the Minister 
in his reply that it is the lookout of the Special Purpose Vehicle to identify and locate the 
places for establishing the parks. I am inclined to ask that there should be a set of guidelines, 
standard norm with regard to identification or locating the places for parks. If so, will there 
be any chance for discretion? If there is a chance for discretion are there any cases of misuse? 
I would like to know. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, the possibility of misuse of any policy cannot be ruled 
out. It is always there in the realm of theoretical possibility and these things do happen. But 
as far as site selection is concerned; would like to inform the hon. Member that it is basically

would be the most economically viable, most suitabl e. For example if there is a leather

would be in that area where there is minimum infrastructure already available for the beneficial 
utilisation of the resources in the leather factory in that particular State. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: My point is whether you are purely going on merit, objectively. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Yes, Sir. It has to be observed . I would like to assure the 
Member.

National child labour projects scheme  
*183. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether on "World Day Against Child Labour" thi s year, Government formulated 
"National Child Labour Projects Scheme (NCLPS)" for welfare and rehabilitation of children 
below 14 years of age; 

6    Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA]                                 to Questions  
(b) if so, the salient features of NCLPS indicating the  number of districts covered, till 
date; 
(c) the number of occupations processes which are consi dered hazardous, banned by 
Government for employment of children aged between 5 to 14 after 2006, when child labour 
was declared illegal; and 
(d) the budgetary allocations made during 2007-08 for welfare programmes of children 
in comparison to 2006-07 as well as during the Eleventh Plan period? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT 
(SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) and (b) The Government is implementing the National Child Labour Project (NCLP) 
Scheme since 1988. Under the NCLP Scheme, children withdrawn from work are put in 
special schools where they are provided education, nutrition, vocational training, stipend 
and regular health check-ups so as to prepare them in a maximum of three years time to 
join the mainstream education system. The NCLP Sche me is at present being 
implemented in 250 districts of 20 States in the country. 
(c) The Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 19 86 prohibits employment of 
children below the age of 14 years in 15 hazardous occupations and 57 hazardous processes. 
This includes two occupations viz. children working as (i) domestic servants and (ii) in 
dhabas, hotels, etc., which were added in October, 2006. 
(d) the budgetary allocations for NCLP Scheme during 20 06-07 and 2007-08 are Rs. 
127.00 crore and Rs. 175.05 crore respectively. For  the 11th Plan period, the proposed 
Plan Outlay for schemes relating to elimination of child labour is Rs. 3738.91 Crores. The 
same is subject to necessary approvals.

SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister, by when 
would he be able to cover all the districts and States under this Scheme, how many children 
are going to be covered, what is the quality of edu cation and nutrition being given to all 
these children and who is accountable for this entire programme. 
SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES: Sir, our effort is to cover all the districts in the next Five 
Year Plan. Under the NCLP, we would like to have special schools in all the districts of our 
country in the next Plan. As per the 2001 Census, t here are 1.26 crore of economically 
active children in the age group of 5—14. Out of wh ich, approximately, 12.6 lakhs are 
working in hazardous occupations We have been able to get these children admitted into 
schools and 4.57 lakh working children have been mainstreamed to regular education under 
the NCLP. Sir, at present, there are 8,887 NCLP Schools being run in the country with an 
enrolment of 3.4 lakh children. Our effort is to see that parents are helped and see that their 
income is increased through the National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme whereby 
the parents will not be forced to send their children for child labour.

I would also like to know what is the State fund available to this, in addition to the Central 
Fund to make this scheme workable? 
SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES: Sir, as of now about Rs. 127 crores is being spent on this

not able to straightaway give the figure of how much State Governments are spending. I

Blacking out of TV channels by Gujarat Government  
*184. SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARATAIMUR: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that Aaj Tak, NDTV and CNN-IBN were blacked out 
in Ahmedabad by Gujarat Government in October, 2007; 
(b) if so, whether All India Cable Operators Association has filed a complaint against this 
gagging of freedom of electronic and print media; and 
(c) whether Government has devised or is devising effective safeguards so that freedom 
of electronic and print media is not arbitrary denied on whimsical grounds? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) Cable Operators in the jurisdiction of Ahmedabad District were prohibited 
by District Magistrate, Ahmedabad from relaying certain programmes related to communal 
riots of 2002 that were carried by Aaj Tak and IBN-7 TV channels. 
(b)No, Sir. However Cable Operators Federation of I ndia had filed a complaint dated 
21 st  August, 2007 stating that political campaign casse ttes and CDs are being distributed 
through Gujarat Entertainment Tax & Information per sonnel with a letter written on 
departmental letter-head and 'operators are directe d to show these footings on the prime 
time'. Another complaint dated 30 th  October, 2007 was received from the Federation that a 
company called Infinium is using OB Vans and various fibre optic networks to downlink the 
signals of the channel 'Vande Gujarat' from interne t and distributing it using personal 
computers & fibre-optic cables to all the MSOs and cable operators in the State, 
(c) Government fully respects freedom of the electronic and print media. All broadcasters 
are required to abide by the Programme and Advertising Codes prescribed under the Cable 
Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and rules framed thereunder. As regards print 
media it is informed that the Press Council of India is a statutory autonomous body with the 
twin objectives of preserving the freedom of the print media and of maintaining and improving

the standards of News Papers/News Agencies in India  and to inculcate principles of self-
regulation among the print media. The Government follows a policy of non-interference in 
the functioning of the Council which enjoys complete autonomy in its functioning. 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARATAIMUR: Sir, the hon. Minister, in his reply, has stated, 
"Cable operators in the jurisdiction of Ahmedabad D istrict were prohibited by District 
Magistrate, Ahmedabad from relaying certain program mes related to communal riots of 
2002 that were carried by Aaj Tak..." He further says, "Government fully respects freedom 
of the electronic and print media .... The Government follows a policy of non-interference in 
the functioning of the Press Council which enjoys complete autonomy in its functioning." 
So, I would like to now whether the Government of India took any action against those who 
violated the autonomy of the Press Council. 
SHRI PRIYARANJAN DASMUNSI: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the particular incident mentioned 
by the hon. Member, Shrimati Syeda Anwara Taimur, is very important. The Collector of 
Ahmedabad banned the said relaying of Tehalka in 20 02. Some of the journalists of the 
concerned channel came to me. I asked them to give a written complaint in this regard so 
that we could investigate the matter. Rightly or wrongly, I don't know, none of the channels 
gave anything in writing. The powers of a Collector in any district of India are guided by an 
Act, which was passed by Parliament, the Cable Net Regulation Act, 1985. As per this Act, 
if a Collector, in his wisdom, feels something is prejudice to the harmony in the area, which 
he presides, he can order the banning of such things. And, after careful study and investigation 
by my own Ministry, I found that the Collector of Ahmedabad did the right thing. Therefore, 
we do not think that anything was wrong in that. The Freedom of Speech and Freedom of 
Expression is allowed, subject to the guidelines of  the Cable Net Regulation Act, 1985. 
Therefore, in my opinion, it appears to me, not merely as a Minister but also as a citizen of 
this country that if there was some plan or agenda in any quarter to show that constantly and 
create a kind of situation which could polarise one  against the other, the Collector of 
Ahmedabad did the right thing. I support.. ..(Interruptions)...

Act decisively decided that a collector is in command of certain power within the Act which 
we passed in this House. If he feels a particular expose can endanger the situation of harmony, 
he can do so. It is the Parliament who gave the power to a collector. This is one thing. 
Secondly, about this expose and a few others, you may hear me first. A company called, 
Infinium, surreptitiously got a DoT licence for VSAT long before the Gujarat election was 
announced. And, OB-van is to carry from internet, using the PC computer, to encroach and 
access on the channels which are regularly operating through cable network regulation and 
the Satellite on mandatory prime programme or non-prime band. Suddenly, be it STAR TV, 
be it NDTV or any channel, started projecting their Bande Gujarat, an entertainment and

campaign programme of the Gujarat Government. Sir, at that time, a complaint was lodged 
with the Ministry by the Cable Operators Federation of India. I gave due cognizance to it, 
and I found that these allegations were correct. Th e OB-Van started operating here and 
there. Nobdoy knew what happened. Somebody who was waiting to see Kaun Banega 
Crorepati suddenly found that that was not coming, Bande Gujarat was coming. Somebody 
who was waiting for seeing some non-prime programme of DD Bharati found that that was 
not coming, Bande Gujarat was coming. Then we enquired and found that Bande Gujarat 
was being operated as a separate channel through using that particular OB-Van who got the 
V-SAT licence from the DoT, not from our Ministry, and that licence was misused, day in 
and day out, to operate, in this style. Sir, this is number one. 
Number two, we also gathered that just on the eve of election notification, something is 
expected very suddenly—I don't blame anybody nor ha ve I desire to put any blame on any 
company—at that inappropriate time, on the eve of e lection notification, another thing was 
being planned by some other channel to focus it and twist the mind. The channel, has shown— 
I have also seen it—the horrifying story of 2002.I welcome the Members' agitation because 
it deserves more publicity. But, its timing is impo rtant. A polarisation was planned by a 
group very .sincerely, sitting in Delhi and sitting in Ahmedabad. After collecting all this, I 
then read the Cable Television Networks (Regulation ) Act. You must be knowing, Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, that no other Collector of Gujarat State had shown the courage and wisdom 
to know what is going to happen, except the Ahmedab ad Collector. There were many 
other Collectors. Everybody was advised not to ban it, not to ban it. But he was the one 
who strictly adhered to the norms of the Constitution, everything, and stood by it. I examined 
it for three days. Then I asked the channel, 'please give me in writing that you are opposing 
to it, so that I can take action.' But the channel refused to give anything in writing. Just tried 
to build it up. Try to understand the inner meaning also. Then I found that both the OB-Van 
licensee and the operator were operating at tandem. Sir, then by using the power that was in 
my hand, I cancelled the DTH licence of that operator who was doing the clandestine operation 
in this manner and I left the other things to DoT to investigate and inform me of the factual 
position of the matter so that we can take action. This is the background of the episode. Yes; 
the hon. Members from the Left, Samajwadi and other parties have a right to say that 'since 
it was exposed in that way, why do you welcome the ban imposed by Ahmedabad Collector?' 
You should also understand why the Ahmedabad Collec tor did it and why the rest of the 
Collectors did not do it. Later on, the Election Commission also stood by what the Ahmedabad 
Collector did. The Election Commission banned the Bande Gujarat Theme, the manner in 
which they were operating encroaching upon the prim e time of the other news channels. 
This is the factual position. Please try to understand it. It is not intentional and it is not that 
I suddenly become a votary of 2002 communal riots; not at all. The inner meaning is that this 
expose could have been shown even six months back, five months back. I don't mind. But 
just doing it at the time of the Election Notification period and the game plan behind it was 
something which need to be looked at. And they also refused to give in writing saying that 
'since we are affected, why don't you allow us to show it'? No. Because they know that by 
giving in writing, the exposure will come in a bad way and some more investigation will take 
place.

nation is thinking that secularism should win in Gujarat, then you don't compel me to give 
dividend to someone who tries to campaign for a particular ...{Interruptions)...

Initiatives to check crime rate in Metropolitan Cities 
*188. SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether any effective initiatives with planning have been taken by Central Government 
to check the growing crime rate in the metropolitan/big cities of the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAI RS (SHRI 
SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (c) 'Police' and 'Public Order' are State subjects under the Seventh Schedule to the 
Constitution of India and therefore, the State Gove rnments are primarily responsible for 
prevention, detection, registration and investigation of crime and for prosecuting the criminals 
through the machinery of their law enforcement agencies. 
The analysis of crime data in 35 metropolitan/big cities (having a population of i 0 lakhs or 
more) for the last 5 years (2002-2006), indicates v arying trends in respect of crime rate 
including decline in the case of some cities. 
The Union Government, however, supplements the efforts of the State Governments by 
providing them financial assistance for modernizati on of their Police Forces, in terms of 
weaponry, communication equipment, mobility, training and other infrastructure under the 
Scheme for Modernization of State Police Forces. Du ring 2006-07, Rs. 96.43 crore have 
been released to the various States for focused attention on policing metro cities of Hyderabad, 
Bangalore, Chennai, Mumbai, Ahmedabad and Kolkata i n the spheres of surveillance and 
crime investigation, traffic management, special ne eds for security related communication 
systems, PCR van net work, digital radio trunking, etc. as a specific component under +the 
Scheme of Modernisation of State Police Forces. Further, intelligence inputs are regularly

†*187. SHRI ALI ANWAR: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased

SINGH): (a) to (d) Under Bharat Nirman, it is targe ted to connect all habitations having 
population of 1000 persons and above in Bihar with an all weather road by 2009. For Bihar, 
it is targeted to connect 9956 habitations during t he period 2005-09. So far upto October, 
2007, 1297 habitations have been connected and projects for connecting 1733 habitations 
are in progress. 
So far, project proposals for 2959 road works measu ring 15225 km. and valued at Rs. 
5367.26 crore have been cleared by the Ministry of Rural Development under Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), Rs. 1381.27 crore have been released for PMGSY 
projects in Bihar Rs. 1167.31 crore has been spent upto October, 2007.

provision for three tier Quality Control Mechanism.  The first two tiers of the Quality 
Control Structure are overseen by the State Quality  Coordinators, appointed by the State 
Governments. The first tier of quality control mechanism is in-house quality control at the 
level of the executing agencies. Field laboratories  are established by the Contractors and 
mandatory tests on the quality   of material and workmanship are conducted under

*191. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased 
to state:

benefit of extension of their retirement age, where as regular officers have been given this

reckonable service as recommended by the AV Singh Committee. 
Schemes for welfare of weavers 
†*192. SHRI RUDRANARAYAN PANY: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the details of schemes being executed by Government at present for the welfare of the 
weavers; 
(b) whether any scheme, namely Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana (DDHPY),

the 11th plan, the Government of India is implement ing following schemes for welfare of 
hand loom weavers:

(i) Health Insurance Scheme 
The scheme covers not only the weaver but his wife and two children also. It covers all 
pre-existing diseases at well as new diseases. The annual limit per family is Rs. 15000/- out 
of which Rs. 7500/- is for OPD. Besides hondloom weavers, ancillary Handlooms workers 
also eligible to be covred under the scheme

(ii) Mahatma Gandhi Bunkar Bima Yojana

accidental death as also disability. The benefits range from Rs. 60,000 to Rs. 1.5 lakh. 
(2) INTEGRATED HANDLOOMS DEVELOPMENT SCHEME is under consideration 
of the government. The scheme is formed by subsuming some of the components of Deen 
Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana, Integrated Handloom Training Project, Workshed-cum-

& corporations through publicity related activities'and participation in International Exhibitions. 
Buyer-Seller Meets etc.

The objective of the Mill Gate Scheme is to provide  all types of yarn to the handloom 
weavers' organizations at the Mill Gate Price.

The Scheme has been formulated with the objective of providing skill upgradation of the 
handloom weavers through training, workshops and ex hibitions, design development 
documentation of traditional designs and providing linkage and meeting the marketing 
requirements. It has also been decide to conduct th e third all India Handloom Census and 
issue Identity Cards to the handloom weavers. 
(b) and (c) The Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana (DDHPY) was introduced in

Opposition to foreign investment in retail trade  
†*194. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether some of the States like Kerala have not allowed to open Western style retail 
food stores; 
(b) the steps taken by Government for the protection of  traditional retail business of 
India; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Indian retail trader s are opposed to allowing the retail 
trade open for foreign investors; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken by Government for the redressal of their objections? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL NATH): (a) and 
(b) While Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is not allowed in retail trading except for retailing 
of Single Brand Products, there is no restriction o n domestic retailers to establish retail 
stores in the country. However, certain States like Kerala have, in principle, opposed entry 
of domestic companies in the retail sector in the States.

allowing FDI in retail trade.

WTO in Doha  
†856. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be 
pleased to state: 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi . 

40    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
(a) whether it is a fact that the biggest obstruction in die progress of present development 
Round of WTO in Doha is the obstinacy of developed countries that they are not ready to 
reduce the huge subsidy which they are giving to farmers in their countries; 
(b) if so, the measures suggested by developed countries to solve this problem; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to ensure livelihood of farmers and employment to 
workers at a time when India's target is to achieve nine per cent growth in economy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY 
OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) Domestic 
support issues and market access are key aspects of  the agriculture negotiations under the 
Doha Round of trade negotiations in the World Trade  Organisation (WTO). On 17 July 
2007, the Chairman of the WTO's Committee on Agricu lture-Special Session brought out 
Draft Modalities on Agriculture, which, inter alia, proposes a tiered formula for reduction 
of Overall Trade-distorting Domestic Support (OTDS). This implies reductions in OTDS by 
the European Communities and die United States of A merica by 75-85% and 66-73% 
respectively. The text further proposes higher cuts by developed countries which have high 
OTDS of 40% or more of the total value of their agr icultural production. Multilateral 
discussions on the Draft Modalities are being held since September 2007. 
(c) The needs and interest of the developing and le ast-developed, countries are at the 
heart of the Doha Work Programme. A substantial and effective reduction in domestic support 
and tariffs in agriculture by developed countries w hile enabling developing countries to 
protect and promote the interests of their low inco me and resource poor farmers is a key 
priority for India in the negotiations. The flexibilities available to developing countries would 
be utilized for protecting the sensitive sectors in  non-agriculture from the impact of tariff 
reductions or bindings. 
With a view to protecting the livelihood of farmers and increasing agricultural production, 
the Government has adopted a multi-pronged strategy including initiatives such as launcing 
of the National Horticulture Mission, micro-irrigation, balanced use of fertilizers, development 
of marketing infrastructure etc. A comprehensive credit policy was announced on 18 June 
2004 for increasing the flow of credit to the agriculture sector. Two new Schemes, that is, the 
National Food Security Mission to increase production of rice, wheat and pulses and Rashtriya 
Krishi Vikas Yojana have been launched with the obj ective of incentivising the States to 
increase public investment in agriculture and allied sectors.

†870. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI:  
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per the Doha Declaration 2001 the rounds of World level talks with 
regard to trade-development had to be completed by December, 2004; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

Written Answers to [28 NOV. 2007] Unstarred Questions   51 
(b) if not, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the rounds of the ab ove mentioned talks has not so far 
been completed; 
(d) the number of talks taken place for this purpose; and 
(e) what are the factors responsible for the failure of these talks? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY 
OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) to (e) The Doha Round 
of multilateral trade negotiations were launched at the fourth Ministerial Conference of the 
World Trade Organization (WTO) held in Doha in November 2001. The Doha Ministerial 
Declaration had provided that these negotiations shall be concluded not later than 1 January 
2005. These negotiations which were stalemated at the fifth WTO Ministerial Conference 
held in Cancun in September 2003 re-commenced after the 1 August 2004 Decision of the 
WTO General Council adopting the Framework Agreemen t. Commonly called the "July 
Framework", this Decision provided a road map for the WTO negotiations up to the Sixth 
Ministerial conference of the WTO in Hong Kong and China, which was subsequently held 
in December 2005. The Hong Kong Ministerial Declaration resolved to conclude the WTO 
negotiations in 2006. 
These negotiations were suspended on 24 July 2006 i n view of the wide gaps in the 
positions of WTO Members, particularly in respect of market access and domestic support 
issues in agriculture. In view of this, the negotiations could not conclude by December 2006 
as decided at Hong Kong. 
Since the failure in July 2006, the WTO Members hav e been holding consultations at 
both Ministerial and Senior Official level in bilateral, plurilateral and multilateral formats 
with a view to making progress in all areas of the negotiations. As a result, the negotiations 
resumed on 7 February, 2007. On 17 July 2007, the Chairmen of the WTO's Committee on 
Agriculture (Special Session) and the Negotiating G roup of Market Access brought out 
Draft Modalities on Agriculture and Non-Agricultural Market Access (NAMA) respectively. 
Multilateral discussions on the two Draft Modalities texts are being held since September 
2007. Negotiations in Agriculture, NAMA and all other areas including Services and Rules 
are being held in accordance with the mandate contained in the Doha Ministerial Declaration; 
the 1 August 2004 Decision of the WTO General Council adopting the Framework Agreement; 
and the Hong Kong Ministerial declaration of December 2005. 
Throughout the negotiations, India has been working constructively with coalition partners 
in Developing Country groupings, such as the G-20 t he G-33, G-90, and NAMA 11 to 
achieve an outcome that would appropriately reflect the development dimension of the Doha 
Round Mandate.

(CSO), the production of only two industrial groups, namely, Metal Products & Parts (with 
a weightage of 2.81%) and Paper & Paper Products (with a weightage of 2.65%) registered

Liberalized arrest and bail procedure  
910. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ministry of Draft National Policy on Criminal Justice proposes that arrests should 
be restricted and the bail procedure liberalized to avoid short term imprisonment and to check the 
rising prison population in prisons in the country; 
(b) whether Supreme Court in April, 2007 summoned Home Secretaries of 10 States after taking 
serious note of the States not heeding its repeated orders asking for release of thousands of lifers 
languishing in jail despite spending more than 14 years behind bars; 
(c) the steps State Governments are considering to take; and 
(d) by what time a final decision for introducing legislation would be considered? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. 
RADHIKA SELVI): (a) A Committee constituted under the Chairmanship of Prof. Madhawa 
Menon, in its Report on Draft National Policy on Cr iminal Justice submitted to the 
Government, has inter alia, suggested that it is important to restrict arrests perhaps with warrant 
only and that bail, being a legal right, has to be liberally granted unless it is shown that it will be 
prejudicial to the search for truth or to the administration of justice. 

82    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
(b) and (c) In the Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 135 of 2003 titled Anil Sharma Vs. State of Haryana & 
Ors., the Supreme Court of India vide its order dated 28.3.2007 summoned Home Secretaries of States 
of Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, 
Meghalaya, Nagaland, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tripura, Uttarakhand and directed the States to file affidavit. 
The Supreme Court has taken into account the affidavits filed by these States. No verdict has 
been pronounced by the Hon'ble Court. 
(d) The Draft Policy has been circulated to all the  State Government for their views/ 
comments as the Criminal Law and Criminal Procedure are on the Concurrent List of the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution of India and are administered by the State Governments Implementation 
of recommendations is subject to receipt of views from the State Governments and Central 
Government taking a holistic view on the recommenda tions and view of the State 
Governments for which no time-frame can be fixed.

accidents; scientifically analyzing road accidents on various important parameters and 
identification of black Spots; segregation of fast moving traffic from slow moving traffic; 
provision of bus bays, yellow boxes, bus boxes etc.  on city roads; introduction of traffic 
signals/blinkers in accident-prone areas; introduction of Area Traffic Control System to ensure 
safe and smooth flow of traffic; prosecution of tra ffic violator through Interceptors, Red

Statement 
Main findings of Global Employment Trends for Women 
The Main findings of Global Employment Trends for Women Brief, March 2007 are as 
follows:— 
* In absolute numbers, more women than ever before ar e participating in labour 
markets worldwide. They are either in work or actively looking for a job. 
* During the past ten years, the labour force participation rate (the share of working-
age women who work or are seeking work) stopped growing, with many regions 
registering declines. This reversal is notable, even though it partially reflects greater 
participation of young women in education. 
* More women than ever before are actually in work. T he female share of total 
employment stayed almost unchanged at 40 percent in 2006 (from 39.7 per cent 
10 years ago). 
* At the same time, more women than ever before are unemployed, with the rate of 
women's unemployment (6.6 per cent) higher than that of men (6.1 percent). 
* Women are more likely to work in low productivity jobs in agriculture and services. 
Women's share in industrial employment is much smal ler than men and has 
decreased over the last ten years. 
* The poorer the region, the greater the likelihood t hat women work as unpaid 
contributing family members or low-income own-accou nt workers. Female 
contributing family workers, in particular, are not  likely to be economically 
independent. 
* The step from unpaid contributing family workers or low-paid own-account worker 
to wage and salaried employment is a major step tow ard freedom and self-
determination for many women. The share of women in wage and salaried work 
grew during the past ten years from 42.9 per cent in 1996 to 47.9 per cent in 2006. 
However, especially in the world's poprest regions,  this share is til! smaller for 
women than for men. 
* Young women are more likely to be able to read and write than 10 years ago. But 
there is still a gap between female and male educat ion levels. And there is 
considerable doubt that women get the same chance as men to develop their skills 
throughout their working lives.

Dismal State of Rural Infrastructure  
980. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether over a decade after the introduction of economic reforms, the scenario on the rural 
infrastructure front continues to be dismal as there is no substantial decrease in the number of poor 
people despite a plethora of rural development schemes launched by Government; 
(b) whether rural infrastructure report of the National Council of Applied Economic Research 
has pointed that 40 percent of the villages are still without a road link; 
(c) what are the other main points in the report; and 

Written Answers to [28 NOV. 2007] Unstarred Questions    131 
(d) by what time Government is likely to accept and implement the suggestions made in the 
report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVE LOPMENT 
(SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) to (d) The Ministry  of Rural Development 
implements a number of schemes for poverty alleviation, employment generation, creation of 
rural infrastructure and amenities in rural areas. To improve further rural infrastructure, a major 
plan for rebuilding of rural India, which has now b een conceived as a business plan called 
'Bharat Nirman' is being implemented over a period of four years 2005-2009. The six components of 
the Bharat Nirman are, village electrification, provisioning of safe sources of drinking water, 
village connectivity by telephone and all-weather roads, creation of additional irrigation capacity 
and construction of house for rural poor. The Ministry of Rural Development is implementing 
three of the six components of Bharat Nirman i.e., rural roads, rural housing and rural drinking 
water Supply. Another ambitious schemes taken up from 2nd February, 2006 by the Government is 
National Rural Employment Guarantee, which envisage s to provided 100 days guaranteed 
employment to each rural household each year, those who want to take up manual work. 
On account of implementation of above programmes an d other developmental schemes, 
there has been general improvements. As per the national Sample Organization's 61st round of 
the consumer expenditure data for 2004-2005, the po verty ratio for rural areas declined to 
28.3% as against 37.3% in 1993-94. The findings of the concurrent evaluation of self 
employment programme namely Swaranjayanti Gram Swar ozgar Yojana (SGSY)-2002, 
reveals that 15.09% members sampled swarozgaris of Self Help Groups (SHGs) and 37.24% 
sampled individual swarojgaris crossed the poverty line. 
The National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) has recently published a 
report regarding creation of infrastructure facilit ies in rural areas titled "INDIA Rural 
Infrastructure Report" 2007. The report broadly cov ers the sectors of telecommunications, 
power, roads and transport, water and sanitation. T he report estimated an investment of Rs. 
1,58,313 crore needed for full coverage at 2002-03 prices. Besides the sectoral 
recommendation, the Report recommended new approach es through promoting local 
initiatives, offering micro-finance to build demand , encouraging private providers, 
decentralizing regulations, decentralizing fiscal authority and targeting subsidies.

†981. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Minis ter of RURAL

these factors? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVE LOPMENT 
(SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) The Planning Commis sion uses a poverty line 
based on per capita consumption expenditure as the criterion to determine the persons living 
below the poverty line. It does not take into consi deration income for determining poverty

(b) No, Sir. The State-wise poverty lines differ on account of inter-state price differential. The latest 
estimate of poverty lines in rural and urban areas available for the year 2004-05, is given in 
Statement (See below). 
(c) The poverty line adopted by the Planning Commission is defined as per capita consumption 
of Rs. 49.09 per month in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per month in urban areas at 1973-74 prices at 
national level. These correspond to a basket of goods and services anchored on a norm of per capita 
daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas. The national level 
rural and urban poverty lines (in 1973-74) are disaggregated into state-specific poverty lines using 
state-specific price indices and inter-state price differentials. These state-specific poverty lines of 
1973-74 are updated for the later years using state-specific Consumer Price Index of Agricultural 
Labourers (CPIAL) in the rural areas and Consumer Price Index of Industrial Workers (CPIIW) in the 
urban areas following the methodology contained in the report of the Expert Group of 'Estimation of 
Proportion and Number of Poor*. The national poverty lines in later years are worked out as an interpolated 
value from the national level consumption distribution obtained from the NSS consumer expenditure 
data and the national level poverty ratio. The national level poverty ratio is estimated as an 
average of state-wise poverty ratios.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) Government of India has t wo Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes, namely Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) and Central Rural 
Sanitation Programme (CRSP) to supplement the efforts of the State Government for providing 
water supply and sanitation services in rural areas. Each State Government, including Uttar 
Pradesh and Uttarakhand, is competent to plan, sanction, implement and execute rural water 
supply and sanitation schemes from the funds provided under ARWSP and CRSP. 
(b) As on 1.4.2007, as per ARWSP norms for coverage there are 2,57,385 Fully Covered 
(FC) and 1,722 Partially Covered (PC) habitations in Uttar Pradesh. In Uttarakhand, there 
are 12,852 FC and 5,077 PC habitations in the State. All 70 districts in Uttar Pradesh and 13 
districts in Uttarakhand have been covered under Total Sanitation Campaign. 
(c) Since the State Government are empowered to plan sanction, execute and implement 
the water supply schemes, the involvement of villagers and rural based NGOs in the planning, 
construction and operation of their water delivery systems has been left to the State 
Governments to decide. TSC guidelines permit engage ment of NGOs and Voluntary 
Organizations in TSC projects for various activities. However, their engagement is decided 
by the respective project implementing agencies in the States.

conceived as a plan to be implemented in four years, from 2005-06 to 2008-09 for building 
rural infrastructure in all parts of the country un der which all uncovered and slipped-back 
habitations are to be covered and water quality problem is to be addressed.

People living below poverty line in Haryana 
†993. SHRI AJAY SINGH CHAUTALA: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the present definition of poverty line in the country; 
(b) the total number of people living below poverty line at present in Haryana and what is 
its district-wise percentage in the total population of the State; and 
(c) whether Government proposes to increase or decrease the present levels of the poverty 
line parameter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) The poverty line adopted by the Planning Commission is defined 
as per capita consumption of Rs. 49.09 per month in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per month in urban 
areas at 1973-74 prices at national level. These correspond to a basket of goods and services anchored 
on a norms of per capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban 
areas. The national level rural and urban poverty lines (in 1973-74) are disaggregated into state-
specific poverty lines using state-specific price indices and inter-state price differentials. These 
state-specific poverty line of 1973-74 are updated for the later years using state-specific Consumer 
Price Index of Agricultural Labourers (CAPIAL) in the rural areas and Consumer Price Index of 
Industrial Workers (CPIIW) in the urban areas following the methodology contained in the report of 
the Expert Group of 'Estimation of Proportation and Number of Poor". The national poverty lines in 
later years are worked out as an interpolated value from the national level consumption distribution 
obtained from the NSS consumer expenditure data and the national level poverty ratio. The national 
level poverty ratio is estimated as an average of state-wise proverty ratios. The estimate of national 
level poverty line, therefore, is implicit. 
(b) The latest estimates of the incidence of poverty is  available for the year 2004-05, 
based on the large sample survey on household consu mer expenditure conducted by the 
National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) in its N SS 61st Round (July, 2004-June, 
2005). According to the estimates based on this sur vey, the total number of persons living 
below the poverty line in Haryana is 32.1 lakh duri ng 2004-05.District-wise estimates of 
poverty are not available. 
(c) No, Sir, There is no such proposal at the movement.

Statement-II  
Important steps taken by the Government to boost cotton production  
(i) To improve productivity and quality of cotton f or manufacture and export of 
competitive downstream textiles products, Government launched the Technology 
Mission on Cotton (TMC). The Mission has achieved s uccess in increasing 
productivity and reducing contamination through the upgradation of cotton market 
yards and the modernisation of Ginning & Pressing factories. 
(ii) The Technology Upgradatron Fund Scheme (TUFS) was launched to facilitate the 
modernisation and upgradation of the textiles indus try in the organised and 
unorganized sectors. The Scheme was further fine-tuned to attract rapid investments 
in the targeted sub-sectors of the textiles industry. The cost of machinery was sought 
to be brought down by reducing the customs duty on imports. 
(iii) For the speedy modernisation of the textiles processing sector, Government 
introduced, w.e.f. 20.04.05, a credit linked capital subsidy scheme @ 10% under 
TUFS, in addition to the existing 5% interest reimbursement. 
(iv) to provide the textiles industry with world-cl ass infrastructure facilities to set up 
their textiles units that would meet international environmental and social standards, 
a Public Private Partnership (PPP) based Scheme kno wn as the "Scheme for 
Integrated Textile Park (SITP)" was introduced in August 2005. 
(v) In 2004-05 Budget, the entire textiles sector, except for man-made fibre and filament 
yarn, was provided optional exemption from excise duty. 
(vi) To facilitate the import of state of the art m achinery to make Indian products 
internationally competitive in the post quota regime, in the Budget for 2005-06, the 
customs duty on textiles machinery was brought down to 10%. Only 23 machinery 
items appear in List-49, which attracts a Basic Customs Duty (BCD) of 15%. The 
concessional duty of 5% continues on most machinery items. 
(vii) In the Budget for 2005-06, 30 knitting and kn itwear items were de-reserved. This 
would facilitate the setting up of large sized mode rnized units to meet the 
international competition. 
(viii) Government launched the Debt Restructuring S cheme w.e.f. Sept, 2003 with the 
principal objective of permitting banks to lend to the textiles sector at an 8-9% rate 
of interest. 
(ix) Government has allowed 100% Foreign Direct Inv estment in the textiles sector 
under the automatic route. 
(x) Government has de-reserved the readymade garments, hosiery and knitwear from 
the SSI sector so that large scale investment is encouraged in these sectors.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Demand for special recruitment drive and relaxation in qualification for 
people living on Indo-Pak Border in Jammu and Kashmir 
SHRI T.S. BAJWA (Jammu and Kashmir): Sir, at presen t, some special benefits and 
reservations in recruitment are provided to the people living along Actual Line of Control in J 
and K. But thousands of other families on Indo-Pak border have been denied these facilities. I 
would like to point out that since 1947 and three I ndo-Pak wars, and subsequently after 
Shimla Agreement, these people were settled on the border. Their agricultural lands were 
taken over by Government laying mines and rendered barren unfit for cultivation. Becuase of 
indiscriminate firing on border, these families cou ld not provide proper education for their 
children. They have no proper and regular means of livelihood. These families are on the 
verge of starvation and facing lot of problems, also. 
I would, therefore, request the Central Government to take up the matter with State 
Government and provide special benefits to the enti re families living in J and K international 
border as has been done in case of people living on Actual Line of Control.  
I would also urge upon the Government to start Special Recruitment Drive particularly in 
BSF, CRPF and Army for the people living on border and relax the recruitment qualification 
from matriculation to middle standard, as a special case, as has been done in other areas of 
the J and K State. Thank you.

Delhi-Samli-Saharanpur Railway Lines

Demand for according classical status to Kannada Language 
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY (Karnataka): As this House is aware, 'Kannada 
Language' is a treasure trove of great literary val ue and antiquity and meets all the 
stipulated criteria for according 'Classical Langua ge' status. Its early texts and recorded 
history belong to 252 B.C. The first Kannada litera ry work, 'Kavirajamarga' was created in 
1850 A.D. and it refers to some writings earlier th an that. The 12th Century Kannada 
Bhakti movement in the form of 'Vachana' or oral ex pression is unparalleled. Its 
contemporary 'Keertana', which subsequently became 'Karnataka Sangeetha', is an 
endearing contribution to Indian music. 
Antique Kannada, apart from being literature and cu lture, also encompassed 
independent work on many aspects affecting life, na mely, medicine, mathematics, 
veterinary science, agriculture, culinary art and e ncyclopaedias, in oral and written forms. 
The epigraphical material in Kannada, numbering ove r 25000 inscriptions in stone and 
copper, are rich in style and content, not found ev en in Tamil inscriptions. The UNESCO 
records Kannada among the prime scripts of the world. 
Kannada ranks among the first ten living languages of the world with a history of 
continuous writing system spanning three millenniums, like Hebrew, Chinese and Tamil. 
Though similar to Sanskrit and Tamil, Kannada langu age has been meted out a step-
motherly treatment and overlooked for 'Classical La nguage' status. There is simmering 
discontent/ resentment among the people of Karnatak a, which is likely to turn violent if the 
question of recognising Kannada as a 'Classical Language' is not resolved expeditiously. I, 
therefore, appeal to the Government to decide the i ssue favourably at the earliest. Thank 
you.

Demand to drop the proposal for extending M.B.B.S. course by one year  
DR. V. MA1TREYAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, the Union Government has announced extending the 
tenure of medial education by one year. Intentional burdening of medical students under the guise 
of rural service is highly condemnable. 
In today's technology driven world with fast paced developments and innovations in medicine, 
for a medical student from rural background to excel, post graduation and specialization is highly 
imperative. The additional one year imposed by the Government will put immense pressure and 
burden on students as they would be thirty by the time they complete their education Thirty years is 
almost half the lifetime of a person. Parents of medical students are concerned and worried, as 
after completing school education by the age of 18, those pursuing other professional courses 
complete it by 23 or 24 years and commence employment, white doctors, even after completing 
education at the age of 30, are doubtful of earning the same as in other professions. 
Even under the existing pattern of education, provision has been made for serving in rural areas 
for a few months. The young doctors in this country are more than willing to serve in rural areas, 
provided permanent Government employment is provided to them. 
Under such circumstances, the announcement made by the hon. Minister of Health 
extending the tenure of study by one year for medical students is highly condemnable. The 
students throughout the country have resorted to agitation and even hunger strike. Hence I strongly 
urge upon the Government to drop the proposal to increase the course by one year and instead 
initiate steps to provide regular employment in Government to enable them to serve in rural 
areas.

Review of the allotment of Spectrum Policy to Private Telecom Operators 
SHRI AMAR SINGH (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, the telecom sector is witnessing a phenomenal growth 
in building world-class infrastructure for the rapid growth of the country. However, a few private 
GSM operators are engaged in propagating false agenda in the media. 
These operators have been given spectrum free of co st far in excess of their licence 
entitlement and actual requirement of 6.2 MHz and they have, in aggregate, hoarded over 50 
MHz of spectrum across different circles. The loss to the Government by the inefficient use of 
spectrum by these operators runs into thousands of Crores of rupees. 
In view of the above, I demand a comprehensive review of the excess spectrum allocated to 
them free of cost and also initiate an inquiry by a  Central investigating agency in order to 
ascertainas to how and in what manner they have obtained the additional spectrum and they must be 
compelled to surrender the excess spectrum so as to avoid any revenue loss to the Government.

 Need to take steps for Eradication of Manual Scavenging                                                      
from the Country 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR (Assam): Sir, even aft er sixty Years of 
independence, India is having manual scavengers in some States like Bihar, Assam, Uttar 
Pradesh, Karnataka, Punjab, etc. Most of the developed countries do not have scavengers. It is 
a shame for our country where great man like Mahatm a Gandhiji, who was preaching 
equality to all mankind, has lived. Though India is rich in heritage, culture and has developed 
economically and there is a lot of progress in the field of education, science and technology, 
still we have people below povertyline without having home to live and there are beggars in 
innumerable numbers found in the States. For want of job, the manual scavengers are working 
in this shameful job. 
I would like to request the Government of India to take steps so that the system of manual 
scavengers is eradicated immensely from all the States of our country, and take up schemes 
for construction of sanitary latrines all over Indi a, so that manual scavengers will not be 
required to take up the work of removing night soil. Also, schemes should be made to provide 
alternative job for manual scavengers.

Statement [28 NOV. 2007] by Minister    173 
STATEMENT BY MINISTER The stay of Ms.                                                                       
Taslima Nasreen in India 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL A FFAIRS (SHRI 
ANAND SHARMA): Sir, I rise to inform the House of the Government of India's stand on an 
issue which has attracted considerable public attention in recent days. 
As hon. Members are aware, noted Bangladeshi writer, Ms. Taslima Nasreen, has been in 
India for some time. Throughout history, India has never refused shelter to those who have 
come and sought our protection. This civilisational  heritage, which is now Government 
policy, will continue and India will provide shelte r to Ms. Nasreen. Those who have been 
granted shelter here have always undertaken to esch ew political activities in India or any 
actions which may harm India's relations with friendly countries. It is also expected that the 
guests will refrain from activities and expressions that may hurt the sentiments of our people. 
While these guests are in India, the Union and the State Governments provide them with 
protection. These policies will also apply in Ms. Taslima Nasreen's case.

GOVERNMENT BILLS 
The Sashastra Seema Bal Bill, 2006 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill to provide for the constitution and regulation of an armed force of the 
Union for ensuring the security of the borders of I ndia and for matters connected 
therewith, be taken into consideration." 
The Sashastra Seema Bal Bill, 2006 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 28.7.2006 and 
the same was further referred by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha to the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs on 3rd August, 2006, for consideration. The Committee 
considered the draft report on the Bill in its sitting held on 22.2.2007 and adopted the same. 
The Committee, in the process of examining the Bill  and in finalising its report took up 
clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its sitting held on 8th and 9th January, 2007 and 
made certain recommendations. 
Regarding definition of 'enemy" and 'enrolling of non-citizens', it is proposed to amend the 
relevant clauses in the Bill in the following manner. Regarding the definition of enemy, as envisaged in 
clause 2(1), enemy includes all armed mutineers, armed rebels, armed rioters, pirates, terrorists 
and any person in arms against whom it is the duty of any person subject to this Act to take action. It 
is the same definition, as adopted in the Assam Rif les Act by Parliament in the year 2006. 
Regarding enrolment, as envisaged in clause 6(1) and 6(2), it is proposed to delete clause 6(1) 
which relates to enrolment of non-citizens of India in SSB for a limited period. Clause 6(2) is 
proposed to be renumbered as clause 6 which defines enrolment as persons to be enrolled to the 
force. The mode of enrolment and the procedure for enrolment shall be such as may be prescribed. 
The Bill is now renamed as Sashastra Seema Bal Bill, 2007. 
With these words, Sir, I commend this Bill to this august House for consideration and 
approval.

174   Statement [RAJYA  SABHA] by Minister  
DR. KARAN SINGH (Delhi): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, law and order is becoming an 
increasingly significant and difficult task throughout the country. There are various challenges 
that we face. There is a challenge of Naxalites and  Maoists and there is a challenge of 
communal and caste conflicts, and there are lots of  other crimes which are happening. 
Basically, the responsibility for law and order is with the States. However, the Government of 
India does have a very special role to play and for  that purpose it needs necessary 
instruments, Of course, we have the armed forces — the Army, the Navy, the Air Force — of 
which we are proud and which have done a marvellous job over these decades. 
But, in addition to that, there is a whole array of para-military forces which are there to do 
specific tasks. There is the CRPF; there is the BSF, which is largely in J&K, and the Bangladesh 
border; there is ITBP, which is on the Tibet border ; there is the Central Industrial Security 
Force; there is the National Security Force; there is Assam Rifles; and, there is the RRF. 
However, there is the Special Service Bureau which is now renamed as the Sashastra 
Seema Bal. The Sashastra Seema Bal has now been given the special task, Sir, of looking 
into the Nepal-Bhutan border. I would like to make just one point here. With the situation in 
Nepal remaining very confused and very inflammable, and our border with Nepal being so 
long and so porous, there are reports that the turb ulence within Nepal is beginning to spill 
over into the bordering States, particularly in the States of Bihar and in some parts of Uttar 
Pradesh. Now, I am not going into the details of what is happening in Nepal but clearly the 
Maoist cadres there have contacts with our Naxalite s who are now beginning to call 
themselves as Maoist, so I recall in the Nandigram episode the word 'Maoist' was used, that 
the Maoists are there. The Maoists in Nepal and Maoists in India, also evidently, if they use the 
same term now, it means they are closely in touch. How close their collaboration is a different 
matter. The fact of the matter it that this whole border is becoming increasingly difficult. On the 
one hand, we have the terrorist threat, the East-West axis as it were and then we have the 
Naxalite threat, the North-South axis and India is on the crosshairs of these two particular types of 
problems. In order to deal with this the Sashastra Seema Bal ...(Interruptions)... this is now 
being recast after 40 years, Sir. This was set up in 1963 in the time of Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru. 
Since then this has been functioning under the title of Special Service Burea. But now at last, 
it is perhaps overdue, a proper Bill is being brought forth which regularises, organises this Force 
on proper basis. I would just like to make the poin t that one thing that we must avoid is 
duplication and overlapping activities of these Paramilitary Forces. I have some experience of 
this coming as I do from a border area. There are o ccasional areas with which one is not 
quite sure which force is going to look after what. So, I now suggest that with this new Force or 
renamed Force coming into being, we must be very clear that there is no ambiguity because 
these are dealing with very sensitive issues whether it is Tibet or whether it is Nepal or whether it 
is Bangladesh. Therefore, there must be full coordination. This is number one. 
Secondly, the Forces should be fully filled because  we find that in many of the Forces, 
even today there was a statement that there are some vacancies in the BSF and the CRPF. 
If you create a force, there should not be any vaca npies. There are vacancies in the 
Armed Forces also. But that is a different matter and refers to the Defence Ministry. So, Sir, 
with these comments, I would like to support the Bill and I hope the newly christened Force, 
the Sashastra Seema Bal, will fulfil its functions very effectively. Thank you.

SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal): Sir, we sup port this Sashastra 
Seema Bal Bill, 2006. The Standing Committee had di scussed the Bill elaborately and 
made certain recommendations. The hon. Minister has  also made certain comments 
about those recommendations. It is based on that ac tually that our Party supports this Bill. 
We all know that the Sashastra Seema Bal is charged  with guarding of Indo-Nepal and 
Indo-Bhutan borders and it seeks to ensure that the  standards of efficiency and discipline 
of the force are of high order. Sir, the Special Se rvice Bureau was changed to Sashastra 
Seema Bal with effect from 27th March, 2004. But I would like to point out one thing here 
once again and that is that the Padmanabhaiah Commi ttee made a recommendation for 
the organisation's motivational role for security preparedness in border areas and they laid 
emphasis on it so that the SSB enjoyed goodwill and  popular support in the border areas. 
This point had also come up before the Standing Com mittee; and this special role of our 
border security should be given high importance. I want the hon. Minister to let us know 
the position on this particular point. The Home Sec retary had agreed on this point before 
the Standing Committee. So, I would be glad if the hon. Minister could let us know how 
the Ministry is working on this aspect of the matte r and lay emphasis on this point while 
replying to the debate. The civic action programme,  the national awareness and security 
consciousness of the border people and such aspects  should be given greater 
importance. 
Now, one point was discussed in the Standing Commit tee and that was that there are 
different kinds of BGF working in our country in th e name of Border Security Force and in 
other names also on the Indo-Tibetan border and the ir duties are almost the same, their 
functions are also almost the same. So, why can't w e have one common BGF? This point 
was discussed. In the Standing Committee, the offic ials also placed their views and their 
argument was that the sensitivity of different bord er stretches is different. They had also 
added that cadre management is also very important.  That is why these forces functioned 
in that manner. So, I want the-hon. Minister to explain these aspects also. 
So far as the term 'enemy' is concerned, the Commit tee also made its 
recommendations that a more comprehensive definitio n bringing persons involved in 
illegal and other such activities within its ambit should be there. The Committee had made 
such a recommendation. Lastly, I would like to poin t it out here that Dr. Karan Singh has 
referred to the Maoists issue here. We know that 32  Naxalite-Maoist factions are working 
in the country. Our party's position is very clear that they should leave the arms and join 
the mainstream. So far as Nepal Maoists are concern ed, they have joined in the 
mainstream leaving the arms and amunition. That is our position so far as the Maoists are 
concerned. In our country, in Bihar, in Jharkhand, in certain areas of West Bengal and in 
some border areas of Andhra, we know that regular a ttacks are going on weakening the 
national security. So, this is our position so far as the Maoists are concerned. With these 
observations, we support the Bill. Thank you.

lines. In 1963, the Special Service Bureau was raised in the name of SSB. On 27.03.2004, this

this force will take up the same job in our Border States. That is my question, which I would 
like to be clarified by the hon. Home Minister.

effective to fight with the growing terrorism and stop such activities aiongwith protection of the 
borders.

DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA (Rajasthan): Thank you, Sir, for the kind indulgence. A new 
feather has been added to the resplendent cap of hon. Home Minister by formally giving a new 
name to this old organisation of 44 years vintage. He has already Central Armed Forces under 
his tutelage, CRPF being the oldest one, BSF, ITBP, CISF and Assam Rifles. It is understandable 
that functions in general will be nearly same as of any Central Armed Force except that their 
postings will be at different places and for different purposes. This Bill is very well drafted for which 
the hon. Home Minister deserves kudos and congratulations. I wish the other Central armed 
police organisations also got the benefit of this Bill in redrafting or restructuring their old structure. 
However, as far as this organisation is concerned, as has been already pointed out, it was a bureau 
earlier, with a very special intention and purpose. Now, it is not a bureau; it is an armed force now. 
Character has been definitely changed. As it was pointed out, earlier, it was a kind of collection of 
intelligence, espionage, counter espionage, preparing self-defence groups. It was the same kind of 
covert organisation as is usually under Intellegance Bureau or other bureaus. Now, it is an open 
organisation with an armed structure, with a very specific duty, with a very new role of border 
guarding force of two borders, Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan. As has been very well 

182   Statement [RAJYA SABHA] by Minister  
pointed out by hon. Members, these international borders are very important for us. They are very 
sensitive for us also. But, unfortunately, they are porous and because of their being porous, they are 
open to infiltration, smuggling, terrorist activities, etc., because, as the hon. Home Minister knows so 
well, criminals respect no international borders. So, cross border anti-national activities shall have to 
be very specifically watched and cared for by this new organisation. It shall have to act as a watchdog 
for guarding these two very sensitive borders. As has been rightly pointed out by another hon. Member, 
as this is the latest new armed unit, its training, its equipment, its arms are expected to be of better 
order than the earlier ones, and, I am sure, the hon. Home Minister will ensure that. It need not be 
emphasised that along with armed posture, this new force has to keep a friendly face with border 
villages, and amicable relations have to be developed with them because without that, a border cannot 
be guarded. No armed force can guard a border without the help of people living on that border and 
without those people having patriotic sentiments for the security of the nation. 
I will like to sound a word of caution, Sir, on two or three points. One is the rate of attrition. 
Somehow, It has to be secured that rate of attrition in this new force is not as bad as it is in old forces. I 
am sure that the hon. Home Minister is aware that nearly 41,000 border security force personnel, one in 
five in the 2.09 lakh force, have quit their jobs over the last 30 months. It is a matter of very serious 
concern and, I think, the whole House will take cognisance of that. Within 30 months, 41,000 trained 
personnel of BSF have quit their jobs. There must be something which troubles diem. It can be their 
prologned duties. Most of the time they are away from their families. They are not having quarters for 
their families or other kinds of comforts. They face difficulty in getting leave from office. This attrition is not 
peculiar only to the BSF. 
Out of these peronnel who quit the job, 7000 men were deployed along the Indo-Pakistan Border 
and the Indo-Bangladesh Border. They put in their papers in the first half of 2007. Nearly 16,200 quit 
in 2006 and more than 17,000 in 2005. It was not peculiar for one year. A trend has been set and it 
has to be looked into why it is there. And, primarily, those who quit were constabulary who spent prime 
of their life at the border. The annual attrition rate is 8 per cent. I am quoting from statistics. But the 
BSF peronnel are not the only personnel affected by that. 
My concern is that this infection should not spread to the new force which you have now renamed 
and which you are bringing up through a new legislation. Nearly 2000 personnel quit the CRPF. It is a 
force of 2.48 lakh personnel. It is the oldest vintage force of your armed organisations. Nearly 1,500 
personnel quit the Assam Rifles. Nearly 1,000 peronnel quit the Central Industrial Security Force. 
More alarming is the suicide rate in the BSF which is three times higher than the Army. Last year, 
41 BSF personnel committed suicide. Suicide rate in the BSF is 20.5 per lakh against 6.6 per lakh in 
the Army. Why is it so? It is for you to look into it. But it is a matter of alarm. 
Obviously, as I am able to visualise, our security forces have had enough of tough life, long 
periods away from home and few rewards. They are not satisfied with the role they are playing. This 
infection should not spread to the new force which you are raising. I thought I would bring this fact to 
your notice. You may already be aware of it. What is the tension which is eating into them?

Statement [28 NOV. 2007] by Minister   185 
Another point that I would like to rise is not directly related to this legislation itself. As far 
as unified command is concerned, we have got a unif ied command. It was considered not 
desirable to have a unified command. Our predecessor Governments had wisely not opted 
for a unified command. But thereafter the Government has a unified command. I would like to 
know whether the Home Ministry has got any informat ion whether the unified command is 
going to be disbanded. In fact, I feel that there should not be any unified command among our 
Armed Forces. 
As far as transportation of Paramilitary Forces and  Armed Forces is concerned, their 
transportation is an important matter of concern. You must have heared, Sir, that there were 
conflicts between the civilians and the people from Paramilitary Forces while travelling in the 
trains. There are conflicts and fights in the railway stations. Therefor, I would suggest that, 
as far as possible, separate bogies should be attached for the transportation of the Armed 
Forces. I know that there are arrangements. But sti ll they are not sufficient. There should 
be sufficient separate bogies for transportation of the Armed Forces from place to another. 
Secondly, now the airlines have become very cheaper and, I think, the Forces can travel 
from one place to another by airlines, of which the fares are not much more than 2nd AC or 
3rd AC. Therefore, this option should also be explored. 
Another aspect is relating to the communication system. Earlier members of the Armed 
Forces hardly used to have any mode of communicatio n with their family members. They 
used to write letters and the letter used to reach their houses after 15 or 20 days; and there 
was joy in the family when they received the letters, etc. Now, on account of the improvements in 
the communication system, the Armed Forces can acce ss their family members easily. I 
think, there is further scope for improvement on th is aspect. I would suggest that there 
should be visual communication between the members of the Armed Forces and their families. 
Video communication between the members of the Armed Forces and their families should 
be allowed, from time to time, so that they can see their family members in their houses on 
the video system. This will give them a feeling that they have gone to their houses, met their 
children and other family members. 
Another aspect which I would like to mention is that we should try to avoid corruption. In 
many departments of the Armed Forces, especially in the purchase of commodities and food 
items, we find that several cases of corruption are  going on. They should be minimized 
because the image of the Armed Forces — it is not a  question of corruption only — among 
the civilized society gets tarnished. We see them i n a different light and this should not 
happen. 
Lastly, I would like to stress, as has already been stressed by many hon. Members from 
time to time, that we should try to use the service s of the Armed Forces and Paramilitary 
Forces for the purpose of controlling law and order situation to a minimum extent because 
when the Armed Forces or the Paramilitary Forces wi eld lathis or arms, it is the civilian 
society which accuses them. The civilian society accusing the members of the Armed Forces 
is not a healthy thing. Therefore, to keep them away from accusations by the civilian society, 
we should see to it that the services of the Armed Forces are used very rarely to control the 
law and order situation. Thank you.
